Not clearly. Reach isn't the binding constraint for a stablecoin; liquidity depth, peg defense, and trust are, and a 12-chain launch works against all three.

- **Liquidity fragmentation:** Spreading initial liquidity and incentives across 12 venues leaves each pool thin. Thin pools depeg easily and slip on size, and an early depeg is hard to recover from reputationally.
- **Risk surface:** Each chain adds its own contracts, bridge or messaging dependency, oracle setup, and monitoring and incident-response burden. A single exploit or bridge failure on one chain can damage confidence in the whole asset.
- **Cost and ops:** Audits, market-maker relationships, exchange and DeFi integrations, and compliance work scale roughly per chain. At launch you probably can't staff or incentivize all 12 well.
- **Signal:** Adoption numbers per chain will look weak, which can read as a failed launch even if aggregate reach is fine.

The usual better path is 1-3 chains with the deepest existing stablecoin liquidity and your target users, then expansion triggered by concrete demand such as partner commitments or measurable volume. Use native burn-and-mint issuance (CCTP-style, CCIP, or OFT) rather than wrapped bridged versions, so expansion doesn't fragment supply.

A simultaneous multi-chain launch can make sense if you already have funded market makers and integration commitments on each chain, a cross-chain issuance architecture that's audited and live, and an ops team that can monitor all of them from day one. If that's your situation, say so and the case changes. Otherwise I'd disagree with "clearly best."
